Five tags give those parts their names, and the tags you already know go inside them. ## Predict ```step stage: predict code: page.html#swap insight: "Students expect header, nav and footer to change the look or position; they only name the parts." check: type: predict q: "after.html wraps the same words in header, nav, main, section and footer tags. What changes on the page?" options: - "Nothing you can see" - "The header and footer get coloured bars" - "The footer moves to the bottom of the screen" - "The list of links turns into a row menu" fault: logic misconception: semantic-tags-look actual: "Nothing you can see. These tags look like no tag at all; their names say what each part is." ``` Compare the two files. They hold the same words, but `after.html` has five new tags. What changes on the page? ## Run ```step stage: run code: page.html#after try: { playground: html, starter: "page.html#after", height: 460, boxes: true } insight: "Section tags change nothing on screen; Boxes shows the named parts." check: { type: reflect, text: "I can explain why these tags change nothing you can see." } unlocks: [page-parts] ``` Compare with your prediction. **Boxes** is on, so you can see the named parts.
